unit_label: Module B unit 2 (courseware unit 11), part 1: HRD and its subsystems, job and role analysis, learning and development, systematic approach to training

facts.statement: HRM has matured to cover the totality of human beings. Workers with high job satisfaction love their job: they feel justice in the environment and find in their job variety, challenge, good pay, security, autonomy and pleasant co-workers. The industrial revolution, with its emphasis on quantity output, de-humanised the workplace; the responses were to make work more interesting, valuable and meaningful (motivation), by recognising the emotions, feelings and needs of people and by changing the content of the job. To reach organisational goals, individuals at all levels need the required knowledge, skills, temperament and attitude; the assumption that anyone can perform any job has been discarded as jobs become more complex. An organisation can either upgrade the skills of existing people or get new people with the required skills, and the cost of acquiring new people is always more than the cost of upgrading existing workers.

The courseware traces the changing context for banks: in the 1970s and 1980s HRD went beyond training; the 1990s brought computerisation for operational efficiency, cost reduction and outsourcing; the first two decades of the twenty-first century brought competition from liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation, with focus on customer service. Traditional public sector and old private sector banks faced foreign banks and new private banks that were technologically sophisticated, and responded with core banking solution based operations, business process re-engineering, voluntary retirement schemes, training and retraining, lateral recruitment of specialists, customer relationship management, new delivery channels, back offices, data centres and business process outsourcing, sometimes with international consultants. The Narasimham Committee mooted bank mergers; five associate banks were merged with SBI, Vijaya Bank and Dena Bank with Bank of Baroda, and in 2019 the government announced the merger of ten public sector banks into four. The human impact of a merger cannot be measured by financial numbers.

HRD today is a process by which the employees of an organisation are helped, in a continuous and planned way, to acquire or sharpen capabilities for present or expected future jobs; develop their general capabilities and discover their inner potential; develop an organisational culture in which supervisor-subordinate relationships, teamwork and collaboration among subunits are strong and contribute to employees' well-being, motivation and pride; and develop competencies (knowledge, attitudes and skills in technical, managerial, human relations and conceptual areas). The goals set by Rao and Pereira (1986) are to develop the capabilities of each employee as an individual, in the present role and in expected future roles, the dyadic relationship between each employee and the supervisor, team spirit in every unit, collaboration among units, and the organisation's overall health and self-renewing capabilities. HRD systems include learning and development; performance appraisal, feedback and counselling; potential appraisal, career planning and counselling; organisational development; the human resource information system; and talent management and succession planning. HRM broadly has three subsystems: administrative, developmental and maintenance.

Job analysis lists what is required to perform a task or job. It traditionally has three parts, job description, job specification and job evaluation; with the growing complexity of jobs and the link with the wage structure, job evaluation is now treated as an independent exercise and job analysis focuses on the job description (the activities involved) and the job specification (the requirement of the person in terms of qualification and attributes). Job evaluation studies a job to determine the activities and responsibilities it includes, its importance relative to other jobs, the qualifications needed and the conditions of work, and is the base for wage settlements. The three primary types of job analysis data are work activities, worker attributes and work context. Job analysis provides the basis for manpower planning, recruitment and selection, learning and development, performance management, reward and compensation, talent management and succession planning, and career planning.

Pareek and Rao (1986) distinguish: a task is a basic element of a job requiring a person to achieve a specific product, in isolation from others; a job is a complex system of tasks requiring an individual to achieve an overall product, with relationships irrelevant; a position puts an individual in a hierarchical pattern in which those below report to those above; and a role emphasises the pattern of mutual expectations and involves socio-psychological relationships. Task, job and position treat individuals as isolated or as means; role takes the individual into a complex relationship involving job, self and others, and is the relevant concept in HRD. The Role Analysis Technique (RAT) clarifies role expectations and obligations of team members to improve team effectiveness; in analysing a role the Key Performance Areas (KPA) and the critical attributes needed to perform effectively are identified.

Job analysis data come from the job holder (first-hand knowledge, to be validated through other sources), supervisors (a broader view, also used for validation and redesign), customers' feedback (useful where customer satisfaction determines success) and experts or job analysts. Methods of collecting data: the interview, the most popular method (structured questionnaires may be used; the analyst should be friendly, assure the person that the exercise will not harm his or her career, and collect facts rather than opinions); the questionnaire, economical and faster when many job holders perform similar jobs; and observation, including work sampling, videotaping or remote monitoring, which takes more time but gives detailed and accurate data on activities and methods.

A job description contains: job identification (title, alternate title, department, code), job summary, duties performed (the heart of the description: what, how and why of each activity), supervision given and received, relations to other jobs (vertical and horizontal), machine tools and materials, and working conditions. A job specification contains: educational qualification, professional qualification, experience, knowledge and skills, personality characteristics, physical make-up, interests and other requirements.

Learning is the acquisition of knowledge, skills or attitudes through experience, study or teaching; development is the broadening and deepening of knowledge in line with one's development goals. The courseware, following Nadler (1984), labels the three levels of activity: training is learning related to the present job, education is learning to prepare the individual for a different but identified job, and development is learning for growth of the individual not related to a specific present or future job. Separating them clarifies objectives (training should be evaluated for performance improvement, development has no direct performance impact), clarifies expectations of the individual and the superior, and clarifies responsibility: for training the immediate superior, for education and development the central department or the overall HR functionary. Other writers use the terms differently, which does not matter so long as the organisation understands them uniformly.

Adult learning (andragogy) is more learner-centred than child learning (pedagogy), which is teacher-centred. The seven principles of adult learning in the courseware are: self-directed, transformational, experiential, mentorship, orientation and motivation (adults are mostly motivated internally), and readiness. Knowles (Nadler, 1984) groups learning theories into mechanistic or behaviourist (the learner is passive and conditioned to respond to stimuli), cognitive (the learner uses the brain for critical thinking and problem solving) and organismic or humanistic (learning occurs when learners have the freedom to learn and develop their full potential). Decenzo and Robbins (1995) list common assumptions: learning is enhanced when the learner is motivated; it requires feedback; reinforcement increases the likelihood that a behaviour will be repeated; practice increases performance; and learning must be transferable to the job.

facts.statement: The systematic approach to training has five steps: training needs analysis (TNA) and identification of training needs; preparation of a training plan; conduct of the training; evaluation of the programmes and the plan; and selection and development of trainers. TNA draws on performance appraisals, productivity norms, rejects, accidents and mistakes and inspection reports, and on the bank's future business plan; not all performance problems can be solved by training (poor technology, outdated processes and poor working conditions cannot). TNA data should help define the need, identify the solution, specify those needing training and give the planning details. The annual training plan specifies the number of programmes (internal and external), the levels of employees covered, the subjects, the allocation of resources and arrangements for contingencies. On-the-job methods include apprenticeship, job instruction training, understudy assignment, programmed instruments and job rotation.
facts.locator: Printed pp. 211-213, Systematic Approach to Training, Steps 1 and 2

facts.statement: Conducting training begins by spelling out the objectives of the programme, which also guide the methodology and the time allowed (practice time for a skill); the profile of the target group influences the methodology. Methods include readings, lecturettes, experiential lectures, group discussion, participative training, experiential training, case studies, role plays, instrumentation (tests and instruments), simulation games, assessment centres, structured experiences and small groups. The more interactive the method, the more the trainer's ability to handle the data generated matters. Evaluation is commonly done at four levels: reaction (participants' opinions of content, method and trainers), learning (knowledge, skills and attitudes acquired, tested before and after), behaviour (transfer of learning to the workplace, observed in work performance) and functioning or results (effect on the functioning of the organisation, measured as financial benefits or return on training investment, which is hard to separate from other causes). The levels resemble Kirkpatrick's model of reaction, learning, behaviour and results. Trainers may be drawn from operational managers (who relate to actual work but risk a narrow approach) or from professional trainers (who bring a different outlook but may lack industry knowledge); a combination often works, and either needs development of their skills.

payload.title: Why development matters: people, jobs and the cost of skills
payload.core_explanation_md:
Industrial work once treated people as substitutes for machines. Later thinking restored the human side: make work interesting and meaningful, recognise feelings and needs, and shape the job so that it satisfies people as well as output goals.

What do people value in a job? **Variety, challenge, good pay, security, autonomy and pleasant co-workers**, together with a sense that they are treated justly. Workers who are happy at work tend to be creative and committed.

Two hard business facts follow:

- Organisational goals are reached only if people at every level have the right **knowledge, skills, temperament and attitude**. As jobs grow complex, "anyone can do any job" no longer holds.
- When the skills are missing there are two routes: **upgrade the skills of existing staff**, or **hire new people** with the skills. The courseware notes that acquiring new people **always costs more** than upgrading existing workers.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: This is the economic case for HRD: investing in the people already in the bank is usually cheaper than replacing them.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two ways to close a skills gap, and say which is usually cheaper.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Upgrade the skills of existing employees, or recruit people with the skills; upgrading is usually cheaper.

payload.title: The banking context that shaped HRD
payload.core_explanation_md:
The courseware describes how bank HR had to change over decades:

| Period | Pressure | Effect on HR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1970s to 1980s | Growth in the HRD idea | HRD moved beyond mere training |
| 1990s | Computerisation, cost reduction, outsourcing | Training for computer skills; fear among seniors who lacked them |
| 2000s to 2020 | Liberalisation, privatisation, globalisation; competition from foreign and new private banks | Customer service skills; analytics; restructuring |

**Bank responses:** core banking operations, business process re-engineering, voluntary retirement schemes, training and retraining, lateral recruitment of specialists, customer relationship management, new delivery channels, back offices and data centres, outsourcing.

**Consolidation:** the Narasimham Committee mooted mergers; five SBI associate banks merged with SBI; Vijaya and Dena Banks merged with Bank of Baroda; in 2019 the merger of ten public sector banks into four was announced. Merger benefits can be counted in profit figures, but the **human impact** cannot be measured in financial numbers.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: These changes needed carefully thought-out HR policies to help existing staff adapt and learn new skills.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can the human impact of a bank merger not be captured in financial figures?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It concerns people: roles, relationships, fears and the need to learn new skills, which are not measured by profitability.

payload.title: Job analysis: what it is and what it feeds
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Job analysis** is a technique for listing what a task or job requires. Work is the pivot of development, so a good HR manager knows each job well: the activities in it and the kind of person who suits it.

Traditionally it had **three parts**: job description, job specification and job evaluation. Because jobs became complex and are tied to the wage structure, **job evaluation is now treated as a separate exercise**, and job analysis concentrates on the first two:

- **Job description**: the activities involved.
- **Job specification**: what the person needs (qualification and attributes).

The three primary types of data are **work activities, worker attributes and work context**.

**What job analysis feeds:** manpower planning, recruitment and selection, learning and development, performance management, reward and compensation, talent management and succession planning, career planning. It is the basic framework for most HR systems.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: **Job evaluation** compares jobs by their activities and responsibilities, their importance relative to other jobs, the qualifications required and the working conditions, so it underlies wage settlements.

self_check.prompt_text: Which two parts does job analysis now mainly consist of, and where has job evaluation gone?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Job description and job specification; job evaluation is treated as an independent exercise.

payload.title: Task, job, position and role
payload.core_explanation_md:
Everyday speech mixes these words. The courseware, following Pareek and Rao, separates them.

| Term | Meaning | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Task** | A basic element needing one person to achieve a specific product | Isolates the person |
| **Job** | A complex system of tasks that achieves an overall product | Still treats relationships as irrelevant |
| **Position** | A place in a hierarchy; those below report to those above | Can make one person powerful over others and dehumanise |
| **Role** | The pattern of **mutual expectations** between job holder, self and others; socio-psychological | The concept HRD relies on |

Task, job and position treat people as isolated or as machines. **Role** puts the individual into a complex relationship with the job, with self and with others.

The **Role Analysis Technique (RAT)** clarifies role expectations and obligations of team members to improve team effectiveness. When a role is analysed, the **Key Performance Areas (KPA)** and the critical attributes needed to perform effectively are identified.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: In a bank, a branch manager's role includes expectations from customers, staff, controllers and the regional head, not just a list of tasks.

self_check.prompt_text: Which of task, job, position and role is the most relevant for HRD, and why?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Role, because it takes the individual into a complex set of mutual expectations rather than treating the person as an isolated performer or a means to a product.

payload.title: Collecting job data and writing the description and specification
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Sources:** the **job holder** (first-hand, but limited view; validate), the **supervisor** (broader view; validates and may redesign), **customers' feedback** (valuable where customer satisfaction decides success) and **experts or job analysts**.

**Methods:**

| Method | Strength | Caution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Interview** | The most popular; gives a list of technical and behavioural skills | Build trust, assure that it will not harm the career, collect facts rather than opinions |
| **Questionnaire** | Economical and faster for many job holders | Make it simple, in a language people are comfortable with |
| **Observation** (with work sampling) | Detailed, accurate data on activities and methods | More time consuming; the person knows they are watched |

**Job description:** identification, summary, **duties performed** (the heart: what, how and why), supervision given and received, relations to other jobs, machines tools and materials, working conditions.

**Job specification:** educational qualification, professional qualification, experience, knowledge and skills, personality characteristics, physical make-up, interests, other requirements.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Because the job holder knows the job best but has a limited view, the information is validated through the supervisor and, where relevant, customers and experts.

self_check.prompt_text: Which job-data method is most economical when many job holders perform similar jobs?

payload.title: Learning, training, education and development
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Learning** is the acquisition of knowledge, skills or attitudes through experience, study or teaching. **Development** broadens and deepens knowledge in line with one's development goals.

Nadler's three-way label for organisational activities:

| Activity | Aim | Who is mainly responsible |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Training** | Learning for the **present job** | The immediate superior |
| **Education** | Learning to prepare for a **different but identified job** | The central department or HR functionary |
| **Development** | Growth of the individual, **not tied to a specific present or future job** | The central department or HR functionary |

Why separate them? The **objectives** differ (training should show up in performance; development has no direct performance impact), the **expectations** of the individual and the superior become clear, and **responsibility** is assigned. The labels matter less than using them **uniformly** in the organisation.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Other writers use the words differently, calling future-oriented learning development and non-job-specific learning education. Check which usage a question follows.

self_check.prompt_text: A clerk is sent on a course for a post of assistant manager, an identified different job. Training, education or development?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Education (learning to prepare for a different but identified job).

payload.title: How adults learn
payload.core_explanation_md:
Adults are not big children. **Andragogy** (adult learning) is more **learner-centred**; **pedagogy** (child learning) is teacher-centred. Treating adult learners like children by the pedagogical model does not give the desired results.

**Seven principles of adult learning:** self-directed; transformational; experiential; mentorship; orientation (reframing emotions and assumptions about experience); motivation (mostly internal); readiness (shaped by life experience and change).

**Three families of learning theory** (Knowles):

| Theory | View of the learner | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Mechanistic (behaviourist)** | Passive; conditioned to respond to stimuli | Produce the right response |
| **Cognitive** | A brain that can think critically and solve problems | Teach the brain to engage in such thinking |
| **Organismic (humanistic)** | Has the freedom to learn | Develop each person's full potential |

**Common assumptions** (Decenzo and Robbins): learning improves when the learner is **motivated**, needs **feedback**, is helped by **reinforcement**, improves with **practice**, and must be **transferable to the job**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: All three theory families are relevant in an organisation because all three kinds of learning situation occur there. Training for senior executives, for example, may focus on vision and strategy rather than skills.

self_check.prompt_text: Which learning theory family treats the learner as passive and conditioned to respond to stimuli?

payload.title: Systematic approach to training: needs and plan
payload.core_explanation_md:
A planned training system follows five steps:

1. **Training needs analysis (TNA)**
2. **Training plan**
3. **Conduct** of the training
4. **Evaluation** of the programmes and the plan
5. **Selection and development of trainers**

**TNA** looks at present and future needs. **Present** gaps show in appraisals, productivity norms, rejects, accidents and mistakes, inspection reports. **Future** needs come from the bank's business plan (new products, technology, expansion). Training cannot cure every problem: poor technology, outdated processes and poor working conditions are not training problems. TNA data should define the need, identify the solution, specify who needs training and give planning details.

The **annual training plan** fixes: how many programmes (internal and external), which levels of staff, which subjects (and which are left for later), the resources, and arrangements for contingencies. **On-the-job** methods: apprenticeship, job instruction training, understudy assignment, programmed instruments, job rotation.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Whether training is delivered in-house or at external institutions, the same five steps are needed. Most banks run in-house training for bank-specific skills and send people outside for specialised training.

self_check.prompt_text: Which is NOT solved by training: low skill, or an outdated process?
self_check.expected_takeaway: An outdated process: training cannot fix problems caused by poor technology, outdated processes or poor working conditions.

payload.title: Conducting and evaluating training, and the trainers
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Conducting** a programme starts with **objectives**: they decide the content, the time (a skill needs practice time) and the **method**. The profile of the group matters: people with no work experience cannot discuss work cases. Methods range from readings and lecturettes through group discussion, case studies and role plays to simulation games, assessment centres and small-group work. The more **interactive** the method, the more the trainer needs the ability to handle the data the group generates.

**Evaluating** training works at four levels (similar to Kirkpatrick):

| Level | Question |
| --- | --- |
| **Reaction** | Did participants find it favourable, engaging and relevant? |
| **Learning** | Did they acquire the intended knowledge, skills and attitudes (tested before and after)? |
| **Behaviour** | Did they apply it back on the job? |
| **Functioning (results)** | Did the organisation benefit, for example return on training investment? |

The fourth level is the hardest to measure, because benefits are hard to separate from other causes.

**Trainers:** operational managers know the work but may take a narrow, in-bred view; professional trainers bring a fresh view but may lack industry knowledge. A combination often works, and either type needs skill development.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Each higher level is harder to measure but more valuable: a well-liked course (reaction) may still not change behaviour.

self_check.prompt_text: List the four levels of training evaluation in order.
